extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, water-colourists, and art students seeking truthful depiction of clouds
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for observing and representing clouds (central, upper, and rain-cloud regions) in landscape painting, with emphasis on truthful color, form, motion, and use of media (watercolour, chalk, brush).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity through truthful variety
rubrics_metrics.description: A man may reach infinity in every touch and line ... if in these he be truthfully various and obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid implying 'infinity' by mere multiplication or bulk. Achieve profundity by truthful variation and subtle obscurity in individual touches and units rather than by repeating identical elements or increasing sheer number/size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering of the central cloud region (delicate dim flakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole space of the heaven covered with delicate dim flakes of gathering vapor forming a gray interwoven veil which lets the light of the upper sky pass pallidly through their body but never rending a passage for the ray.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict the intermediate veil between central and rain-clouds as faint, universal, and interwoven; let upper light pass through pallidly without hard breaks. Examples cited: Turner's vignettes in Rogers's Italy (pp.115, 223), Voyage of Columbus, Moonlight under the Rialto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color of distant/central clouds (pure aerial grays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Central clouds have pure and aerial grays for their dark sides; their colors are changeful and palpitating because of distance and collected local phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pure, airy gray tones on dark sides of distant clouds; allow subtle, variable color effects (refractions, local mists, sunbeams) to produce palpitating color rather than steady, flat tones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color of rain-clouds (near clouds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nearness of the rain-cloud ... makes its hue of gray monotonous, and (by losing the blue of distance) warm and brown compared to that of the upper clouds; illumined parts are brown, bricky, ochreous; when dense, inky and cold; sulphureous and lurid with thunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render near rain-clouds with warmer, browner grays (bricky/ochreous) for lit parts and inky/sulphureous tones for dense or thunderous conditions. Do not treat them as the same pale blues of distant skies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness and edge of rain-clouds (ragged, spray-like)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rain-clouds often lose almost all definiteness of character and outline; their outline is ragged and torn, rather a spray of cloud sifted by wind than a solid edge; they carry columnar rain hanging like a jagged fringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paint near rain-cloud edges as veils, sprays, and ragged fringes; show hanging columns or veils of rain, waved and bent by wind. Avoid hard, smooth outlines for rain-cloud edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply same laws of light & shade / anatomy to clouds
rubrics_metrics.description: Clouds are regulated by precisely the same simple laws of light and shade as more substantial matter; they are not solid bodies borne about with the wind, but carry the wind with them and cause it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat clouds as formed volumes with articulated chiaroscuro and anatomy. Use drawing and attention to light/shade relationships as you would for any solid form; depict internal motion without losing coherent form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mist and rain-cloud phenomena to modify landscape
rubrics_metrics.description: Drifted smoke, heat-haze, local mists, steaming vapor and related phenomena afford the most effective means for modification of the forms of fixed objects; through the rain-cloud all that is beautiful may be made manifest and what is hurtful concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use veils of mist and rain-cloud to alter perceived scale and character of landscape elements—soften, enlarge, or give mystery—rather than relying only on explicit detail. Apply these effects to create atmosphere, decoration, or concealment where desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid old-master conventions of solid, opaque cloud-volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Old masters often render clouds as massive, convex, opaque globes (like smoke), with hard, smooth edges and no middle measures between white cloud and pure blue sky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not imitate the old convention of impenetrable, round cloud-volumes with clear-cut edges. Prefer veiling, transparency, and gradation; avoid 'boring a hole in the sky' with a flat blue punctured by solid cloud rims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cloud-drawing: give structure, parts, and solidity (Stanfield model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cloud-form is firmly and fearlessly chiselled, with perfect knowledge ... giving the real anatomy of cloud-form with perfect articulation of chiaroscuro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use drawing—chalk, pencil, or lead—to learn cloud anatomy and give each cloud-part structure and solidity. Avoid relying solely on brush-work or leaving areas as accidental paper-lights; aim to 'draw' clouds, not merely suggest them by smear or erased white.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overcharge color or confuse shadows when adding detail
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as modern artists attempt to lay detail upon their clouds, they appear to get bewildered ... overcharge their color, confuse their shadows and dark sides, and end in mere ragged confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When detailing clouds, maintain consistent light-and-shade logic; avoid heightened or noisy colour and overworked brushmarks that break the cloud's form. Use restraint and refer back to structural drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance brush-work with disciplined drawing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The brush is at once the artist's greatest aid and enemy; it enables him to make his power available, but undermines his power unless constantly rejected for the pencil. Many failures arise from neglecting the use of chalk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly practice drawing in simple light-and-shade (chalk/lead) to preserve sense of form; use brush only after strong drawing foundation. Do studies of form-only before depending on brush techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Texture versus plan (Fielding's limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of Fielding's merit depends on particular tricks of execution or a texture rather than a plan of sky; pleasurable effects may fall under dexterous imitation rather than definite thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that texture and brush-tricks can emulate transient effects (especially in watercolour), but strive for considered composition and planning so that texture supports, not substitutes for, structural truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate steam vs smoke in rendering
rubrics_metrics.description: Steam is an artificial cloud in the process of dissipation—irregular, broken, sharp and spray-like—whereas smoke is an actual solid opaque body in the air, with elastic, globular volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render steam with sharp, spray-like, dissipating forms and irregular edges; render smoke as opaque, volumetric globes that do not break up or vanish. Use these distinctions to inform texture and edge work in compositions containing either.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render openings after rain with intense pure azure and melting edges
rubrics_metrics.description: Openings in rain-cloud exhibit the purest blue which the sky ever shows; clouds melt into it with edges passing off in faint white threads and fringes, the blue deepening and broadening here and there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When painting post-rain openings, make the blue intense and variegated (not pale), and let cloud-edges dissolve into delicate white threads. Avoid engraving-like pale blues; the blue may often be darker than surrounding sky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest wind and motion by varied parallelism and non-repetitive curves
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass of cloud may be characterized by severe right lines nearly parallel with each other, but none actually parallel; each line is made of exquisite and varied curves—suggested right-lines formed of varied tangents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey tempestuous motion by implying overarching directional lines composed of many varied curves—avoid repeating identical curves. Let the eye infer parallelism from varied, characterful wreaths rather than literal straight lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express the storm through corroborating landscape details
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute circumstances—falling rain lines, smoke blown every way, cattle standing stiff with heads down, gushing gutters—complete the impression of tempest, fitfulness, and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use secondary details (animal behaviour, flowing gutters, direction of smoke, reflections) to reinforce atmospheric conditions. These elements can tell 'what the storm is and what it has been' and make atmospheric depiction convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use watercolour for transparent, melting, dewy effects—but with considered form
rubrics_metrics.description: One accidental dash of the brush on wet or damp paper will come nearer the truth and transparency of rain-blue than labour in oils; yet Turner combines perfect transparency with considered form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit watercolour's facility for veiling and melting blues and transient effects, but ensure such passage is supported by considered plan and drawing (as Turner does) rather than mere accidental marks.
